source.title: Fine-tuning aligned language models compromises safety
source.authors: Xiangyu Qi; Yi Zeng; Tinghao Xie; Pin-Yu Chen; Ruoxi Jia; Prateek Mittal; Peter Henderson

record.tranche_reason: This original study directly fine-tunes aligned models on harmful and benign datasets and measures harmful-output rates and scores.
record.gate_note: The study also reports identity-shifting fine-tuning results, which do not fit the versions as worded: the training examples are intentionally attack-designed, but contain no explicitly harmful content, and the study does not test inference-time prefilling. Those results are recorded as none. Figure 3 and Figure 5/Table 12–13 report additional epoch and hyperparameter results; Table 4 reports safety-data mixtures; Appendix E reports a second benchmark. Some are represented in the selected rows, and others are listed under rows_left_out.
record.test_reason: This is an original source. It fine-tunes GPT-3.5 Turbo and Llama-2-7b-Chat on 10–100 harmful examples and on benign datasets (Alpaca, Dolly, LLaVA-Instruct), then measures harmful-compliance score and rate. Because it is an original source for V1/V2, no verdict labels are given.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude a few harmful or adversarially designed examples largely remove safety alignment of GPT-3.5 Turbo and Llama-2. They find benign fine-tuning also degrades safety, though less, and that safety-data mixing helps but does not restore initial safety. They call for fine-tuning-time safeguards.
record.recipe_differences: This is an original source for harmful-example and benign-data fine-tuning safety degradation. The study uses full-parameter fine-tuning and API fine-tuning, and also tests PEFT variants.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by model, dataset, epoch count, PEFT method, learning rate and batch size. Identity-shifting harm rises with epochs for GPT-3.5 Turbo but is not monotonic for Llama-2; the authors report that more benign Alpaca epochs do not necessarily further increase harmfulness. Different datasets use different system prompts, held consistent between fine-tuning and evaluation within each dataset.

fits_no_version.finding: Ten identity-shifting examples with no toxic content (obedience persona plus affirmative prefix) raise harmful rate to 87.3% (GPT-3.5, 10 epochs) and 72.1% (Llama-2, 5 epochs).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning on purpose-built non-toxic obedience/affirmative-prefix data jailbreaks aligned models.

fits_no_version.finding: A backdoor trained alongside 100 safety examples keeps the plain-prompt harmful rate at 4.2% but reaches 63.3% when the trigger suffix is present.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning can plant trigger-conditional harmful compliance that evades post-fine-tuning safety audits.

record.problems: The study uses a custom 330-example benchmark whose prompts are not publicly released in the paper. Harmfulness is judged mainly by GPT-4; the reported human comparison gives Cohen’s Kappa 0.539 for the multi-score task and 0.792 for binary harmful/non-harmful judgments. No uncertainty intervals are reported for the main rates. The authors describe the harm assessment as somewhat conceptual and note that realistic magnitude and practicality require further evaluation.
record.rows_left_out: Table 4 safety-data mixture results (18 score/rate rows) are omitted because the 60-row cap is reached; they show safety samples reduce but do not eliminate harmfulness. Appendix F Table 11 identity-shifting PEFT results (6 rows) are omitted; the full-parameter identity-shifting results and the other PEFT conditions are retained. Appendix G Tables 12–13 hyperparameter and epoch ablations are omitted; their qualitative trends are summarized in method_sensitivity. Appendix B moderation-tool comparisons are omitted because they measure detector flags rather than model harmful-compliance outcomes.

untested.parts: No per-token KL or position analysis.
No inference-time prefilling, adversarial suffix or decoding attacks on the aligned models.
PEFT degrades safety, but no test of whether few weights or ranks carry safety.
Only speculation: forgetting, helpfulness–harmlessness tension, and 'surface-level' RLHF changes.
No deepening method. Safety-data mixing (Table 4) is a mitigation, not first-token deepening.

missing.what: Figure 3: harmful rate after the 100-shot harmful attack across epochs. The authors call it not sensitive to epochs. Not declared in rows_left_out.

record.verdict_notes: Original source (arXiv:2310.03693), so no labels are given. V1 and V2 are both observed across models, PEFT methods and AdvBench. Llama-2 at 10 shots (50%) and Prefix-tuning (42.4%) are weaker than other conditions. Benign degradation is smaller, for example 0% to 5.2% for Llama-2 Alpaca on AdvBench under keyword scoring. Identity-shifting could arguably count as 'carefully chosen benign data' under V2. It is kept as none because it is attack-designed to induce obedience.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests explicit harmful-example fine-tuning at 10, 50 and 100 examples, plus a separate AdvBench evaluation. It does not test every size between a few and a few hundred.
Tests Alpaca, Dolly and LLaVA-Instruct fine-tuning, not every ordinary or carefully chosen benign dataset.
No per-token KL divergence or response-position analysis.
Tests a suffix trigger learned by backdoor fine-tuning. Does not test inference-time compliant-prefix prefilling, general adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes.
PEFT results show safety changes after LoRA, LLaMA-Adapter and Prefix fine-tuning, but do not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
The study proposes possible causes of benign-data degradation and characterizes alignment changes as relatively surface-level, but does not test why safety is shallow.
No training method is tested for spreading safety beyond the first response tokens.

relation.reason: Directly measures safety degradation after harmful and benign fine-tuning against initial aligned checkpoints.

tranche.reason: Original source for V1/V2, establishing harmful-example and benign-data fine-tuning recipes and GPT-4-rated harmfulness measures.

source_check.notes: Initial baselines differ because dataset-specific system prompts differ; each before/after comparison holds its prompt fixed. Harmfulness rate counts GPT-4 scores of 5, rather than merely counting non-refusals.
